versioned_rules_reference.scope: Retained versioned reference, not a current-rules audit
rules: 601.2c The player announces their choice of an appropriate object or player for each target the spell requires. A spell may require some targets only if an alternative or additional cost (such as a kicker cost) or a particular mode was chosen for it; otherwise, the spell is cast as though it did not require those targets. Similarly, a spell may require alternative targets only if an alternative or additional cost was chosen for it. If the spell has a variable number of targets, the player announces how many targets they will choose before they announce those targets. In some cases, the number of targets will be defined by the spell’s text. Once the number of targets the spell has is determined, that number doesn’t change, even if the information used to determine the number of targets does. The same target can’t be chosen multiple times for any one instance of the word “target” on the spell. However, if the spell uses the word “target” in multiple places, the same object or player can be chosen once for each instance of the word “target” (as long as it fits the targeting criteria). If any effects say that an object or player must be chosen as a target, the player chooses targets so that they obey the maximum possible number of such effects without violating any rules or effects that say that an object or player can’t be chosen as a target. The chosen objects and/or players each become a target of that spell. (Any abilities that trigger when those objects and/or players become the target of a spell trigger at this point; they’ll wait to be put on the stack until the spell has finished being cast.)

601.2f The player determines the total cost of the spell. Usually this is just the mana cost. Some spells have additional or alternative costs. Some effects may increase or reduce the cost to pay, or may provide other alternative costs. Costs may include paying mana, tapping permanents, sacrificing permanents, discarding cards, and so on. The total cost is the mana cost or alternative cost (as determined in rule 601.2b), plus all additional costs and cost increases, and minus all cost reductions. If multiple cost reductions apply, the player may apply them in any order. If the mana component of the total cost is reduced to nothing by cost reduction effects, it is considered to be {0}. It can’t be reduced to less than {0}. Once the total cost is determined, any effects that directly affect the total cost are applied. Then the resulting total cost becomes “locked in.” If effects would change the total cost after this time, they have no effect.

602.2b The remainder of the process for activating an ability is identical to the process for casting a spell listed in rules 601.2b–i. Those rules apply to activating an ability just as they apply to casting a spell. An activated ability’s analog to a spell’s mana cost (as referenced in rule 601.2f) is its activation cost.

723.1. Some cards allow a player to control another player during that player’s next turn. This effect applies to the next turn that the affected player actually takes. The affected player is controlled during the entire turn; the effect doesn’t end until the beginning of the next turn.
723.3. Only control of the player changes. All objects are controlled by their normal controllers. A player who’s being controlled during their turn is still the active player.

723.4. If information about an object in the game would be visible to the player being controlled, it’s visible to both that player and the controller of the player. If information about cards outside the game would be visible to the player being controlled, it’s visible only to that player, not the controller of the player.

723.5. While controlling another player, a player makes all choices and decisions the controlled player is allowed to make or is told to make by the rules or by any objects. This includes choices and decisions about what to play, and choices and decisions called for by spells and abilities.
723.5a The controller of another player can use only that player’s resources (cards, mana, and so on) to pay costs for that player.
723.6. The controller of another player can’t make that player concede. A player may concede the game at any time, even if they are controlled by another player. See rule 104.3a.

excluded_drafts: Initial fixture API errors and packaged observer multiset/converter mistakes are excluded. An earlier live run correctly rejected missing archive-bound alias/companion reviews. The public card-name B105 annotation is line-specific and leaves the worker AST unchanged. Final native and packaged witnesses use frozen final inputs.
limits: Partial four-player Commander boards, not complete legal-deck gameplay or exhaustive strategy certification.

At most two one-ply legal actions per sampled main phase, fixed seed, existing shared deadline, and a bounded path to the selected second main phase. Intervening main-phase choices, response priority, stochastic fairness, hidden-information strategy and arbitrary turn/combat schedules remain unverified.

Five paid primary sources are covered in heuristic, hybrid and full modes; normal and optionally paid Secret timing is observed. This does not certify all composed or mandatory control decisions, controlled blocking, custom/cyclic controllers, teams or human-agent conversion.

Native costs and world ownership are retained. Sorin's fixed eight loyalty represents an established state; Bracelet equip prefixes are actual native choices and payments. Redundant equip prefixes remain an optimization gap.

Only completed improving plans can survive full-search expiry, and the native picker still validates identity, original score and targets. No completed plan means pass. This does not prove every deadline or plan-invalidation context.

Synchronous preview random scopes restore after exceptions and remain independent in the explicit concurrent tests. Legacy random consumers outside these scopes are not globally certified for concurrent matches.

The two card archive changes remove AI exclusion metadata; no rules script changed. One exact alias and two exact companion wording reviews were carried forward only after full archive comparison and positive/negative native predicate checks.

Catalog construction proves script availability, not full gameplay correctness. Seven nonstarting meld results remain separate. The retained rules reference is versioned, not a current-rules audit; remaining engine callbacks and full Commander interactions still require work.
